verses.note: The first word God speaks to fallen humanity is a question that seeks them out. Before judgment comes a call, and the pattern holds through Scripture to the Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10).

God covers the shame they could not adequately cover themselves. Many Christian interpreters have seen in the skins the first death of an animal on humanity's behalf and a hint of sacrifice; the text does not say so, and others read the act simply as God's care for people he is sending into a harsher world. Either way the image of God clothing sinners runs through Scripture (Isaiah 61:10, Galatians 3:27).

The first mention of grace in Scripture comes at the moment of the world's condemnation. The order of verses 8 and 9, favor first and righteousness second, has long been read as showing that Noah's rescue rests on God's grace, though Genesis also insists that grace produced a righteous life.

Noah's whole household is brought in because of his standing before God. Hebrews 11:7 says Noah built the ark for the saving of his household, and the pattern of God's rescue reaching a family through one person recurs throughout Scripture.

The one who is saved does not seal his own safety; God shuts him in. The same act also marks the end of the time for entering. Jesus' parable of the ten virgins ends with the same image, the door shut when the bridegroom has come (Matthew 25:10).

This is the first remnant in Scripture: a small group preserved through judgment to carry God's purposes forward. The prophets develop the idea (Isaiah 10:20-22), and Paul applies it to the people of God saved by grace (Romans 9:27, 11:5).

Righteousness here is a right standing with God received through trust. The verse shows the way of salvation already at work in Genesis, long before the cross makes plain on what basis God can count the ungodly righteous (Romans 4:5, 23-25).

Lot is not rescued because he runs but because he is seized. The verse is one of the Old Testament's plainest pictures of salvation as God's act of mercy on the undeserving, and 2 Peter 2:7-9 draws the lesson that the Lord knows how to rescue the godly.

Lot is saved for Abraham's sake. The verse shows God's mercy reaching one person because of his covenant with another, a pattern the New Testament fulfills when believers are saved for the sake of Christ.
Jacob's survival is a gift, not an achievement. He lives because God chose not to destroy him, which is the logic of every deliverance Scripture calls salvation.

God's rescue here is physical survival through famine, and it is also the preservation of the line through which the promise to Abraham will come. The vocabulary of remnant and survivors will later carry the hope of rescue through judgment and exile.

The first use of ‘redeem’ in Scripture is a man's testimony that God rescued him from every harm. Before it is the language of the exodus (Exodus 6:6) or of the cross, redemption is a personal rescue by a kinsman who takes responsibility for you.

Jacob's only prayer in the poem is for the LORD's deliverance, placed amid predictions of his sons' wars and struggles. The tribes' future rests on the LORD's salvation, not on their lion strength or their cunning.

Salvation in the Old Testament is first concrete rescue from those who oppress. The small scene at the well uses the same word as the great deliverance at the sea, preparing the reader to see that salvation means being brought out from under a hostile power.

The verse defines salvation as God's own act: he comes down, delivers from the hand of the oppressor, and brings his people into a good land. Rescue from and bringing into belong together, and later Scripture holds both when it speaks of redemption.

The verse gives the Bible's basic vocabulary of salvation: God brings out from bondage, delivers from a hostile power, and redeems as next of kin at his own cost. The New Testament uses the same language of redemption for what Christ does (Galatians 4:4-5; 1 Peter 1:18-19).

The house is spared not because of who lives in it but because of what is on its door. The verse makes God's seeing the blood the ground of deliverance, and Israel's part is to trust the promise enough to act on it.

The last word of the chapter belongs to God's act: the LORD brought Israel out. Israel's obedience has been real and repeated, but the chapter ends by naming who did the rescuing, the note on which the Ten Commandments begin (20:2).
The emphatic ‘I have given’ makes atonement something God provides before it is something Israel performs. Sacrifice is not a bribe offered upward but a provision handed down.
Rescue comes before command. The law's meaning is explained by redemption: God freed a people of slaves and gave them a way to live as free people.
Redemption from Egypt is described as God acquiring a people for himself. The language of padah, ransom, becomes the vocabulary for salvation throughout Scripture (Deuteronomy 7:8; Titus 2:14).
The plea asks God to deliver the whole of what the sufferer is, his one life. Rescue in the Psalms is the saving of a life, not merely relief from pain.
Salvation begins with God's word of comfort to a people who have done nothing to earn it. The sentence is over because God declares it over; the exiles' part is to hear.

The verb basar, rendered in Greek by euangelizesthai, gives the New Testament its vocabulary for the gospel. Here the good news is that God himself has come. When Mark opens with the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ and quotes Isaiah 40:3 (Mark 1:1-3), he claims that this announcement has become true in Jesus.

Redemption in Isaiah is God acting as kinsman to buy back his own. That no silver changes hands does not mean the redemption is costless: the chapter moves straight into the Servant who suffers (52:13 to 53:12). Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19).

Salvation is God's act done in public, before all the nations. The second line of verse 10 is nearly identical to Psalm 98:3. Luke's infancy narrative echoes both halves of these verses: Simeon awaits the consolation of Israel and sees God's salvation prepared before all peoples (Luke 2:25, 2:30-31), and Anna speaks to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:38).
Salvation here is healing and peace, wholeness restored, not merely a verdict. The verse joins the legal (punishment) and the medical (healing) in one sentence.

Israel's return is described as redemption, not escape. God acts as kinsman-redeemer for a people held by a stronger power, the pattern the New Testament uses when it speaks of Christ's giving himself as a ransom (Mark 10:45).

Everything in the new covenant stands on the final ‘for’: I will forgive. The inward law and the universal knowledge of God follow from a relationship God restores by pardon. Jeremiah 50:20 repeats the promise: in those days Israel's iniquity will be sought and not found.

Salvation in this verse is rescue from uncleanness, not only from enemies or exile. Matthew's Gospel says the child will be called Jesus ‘because He will save His people from their sins’ (Matthew 1:21), the same kind of rescue: from the inward captor, not the outward one.
The rescue promised is from sins, not only from enemies. Restoration to the land is not enough; the people must be saved from what brought the exile in the first place.

The petition rests entirely on God's compassion and disclaims any appeal to human merit. The verse is one of the Old Testament's plainest statements that God's people come to him on the basis of his mercy, not their record.

God orders his rescue so that the least protected are saved first and the privileged cannot claim the glory. Paul describes the same pattern when he says God chose what is weak so that no one may boast before him (1 Corinthians 1:27-29).

Life is entered through a gate that must be chosen and a road that must be walked. The verse does not teach salvation by effort, but it does say that following Jesus runs against the current of the crowd.
Jesus addresses the man's sin before his paralysis. The verse does not say the illness was caused by his sin; it says the deeper need is forgiveness, and that Jesus grants it on the basis of faith.

Jesus' table is open to those whom the observant kept at a distance. The meal enacts what the next verses will explain: acceptance into Jesus' company comes before, and as the ground of, a changed life.

Luke's summary is that the people furthest from the Law's standard are the ones drawing near to Jesus. Salvation in Luke moves toward the outsider first, and the verse sets up a chapter in which God's search for the lost is the explanation for Jesus' company.

The son is restored to sonship, not hired as a worker. The robe, ring, and sandals are given, not earned, and they answer the request he never finished making. Salvation in this story is a status bestowed by the father.

Salvation here has a source (God's love), a means (the gift of the Son), a condition (believing), and two outcomes set against each other (perishing or eternal life). Christians debate whether God's saving intention in the gift extends equally to every person; the chapter note sets out the Arminian and Reformed readings.
God's purpose in sending the Son is rescue. Judgment follows in the Gospel, but as the consequence of rejecting the rescue, not as the reason for the mission.

The promise is universal in form, ‘everyone who calls’, and specific in object, the name of the Lord. Peter's sermon will show that the Lord in question is Jesus (verse 36), and Paul quotes the same verse to the same effect (Romans 10:13).
Forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Spirit are the two blessings Peter promises. The same pair runs through the prophets' picture of the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:34, Ezekiel 36:25-27).
Salvation is described as rescue from a generation, a whole way of life under judgment, not only from individual sins. The passive voice makes it something received.
The present participle ‘being saved’ presents salvation as God's continuing work in those who have believed, from forgiveness now to rescue on the Day of the Lord.
Salvation is God's own power at work, received by believing. Because the one condition is faith, the offer is universal, and because the gospel is God's power, no hearer is beyond it.
Salvation is described as a new exodus: as God redeemed Israel from slavery in Egypt, he redeems sinners from the power of sin in Christ Jesus.
Grace and debt are opposites. If righteousness were paid as wages, God would owe it; because it is credited as a gift, God owes no one, and no one can claim it.
A promise that depended on law-keeping would be as uncertain as human obedience. Only a promise resting on grace can be sure, which is the point verse 16 draws.
Only grace makes the promise sure. If it depended on the recipients, it would be as unstable as they are; because it depends on God's giving, it holds for every heir.

Peace with God is Israel's prophetic hope fulfilled. Isaiah promised that the servant's punishment would bring peace (Isaiah 53:5) and announced good news of peace (Isaiah 52:7); Paul says it has arrived through Christ.
Salvation in Paul has past, present, and future tenses. Believers have been justified; they will be saved from wrath. The future is certain because it rests on what God has already done.
Grace is not merely equal to the damage of sin; it overflows it. Whatever was lost in Adam, more is given in Christ.

‘All men’ appears on both sides. Most interpreters, across traditions, read the second ‘all’ as all who are in Christ, as verse 17's ‘those who receive’ indicates, or as describing the scope of the offer; Christian universalists, from some early readers to David Bentley Hart (That All Shall Be Saved, 2019), take it as a promise that all will finally be saved. Paul's argument insists at least that Christ's act is as wide in its reach as Adam's.

The objection only makes sense if Paul's gospel really is free grace; a gospel of earned acceptance would never be accused of encouraging sin. Paul keeps the grace and answers the objection by showing that grace does not merely pardon, it also relocates the person out of sin's territory.
Grace here is not only a favorable verdict but a power under which a person lives. That is why grace is the answer to sin's dominion rather than its excuse.
Eternal life is a gift, not a wage, and it is ‘in Christ Jesus’. The verse compresses Romans 1-6 into one line: sin earns death, and God gives life freely in his Son.
The cry marks the end of self-help. Salvation here is rescue by another, and the future tense points toward the redemption of the body described in 8:11 and 8:23.

Thanksgiving comes before explanation. Paul answers the cry of verse 24 with God's act in Jesus Christ, and chapter 8 will show how: no condemnation, the Spirit's life, and the promised redemption of the body.

Salvation is already and not yet. The Spirit's life is present now because of righteousness, God's saving verdict, while the body still bears the sentence of death. Verse 11 shows how that tension will end.
Adoption is one of the richest pictures of salvation in Paul: not only pardon but a new family, a new name, and an inheritance. Paul uses the same word for Israel's privilege in 9:4.

‘In hope we were saved’ holds past, present, and future together: believers were saved, and what they were saved into is still ahead. Paul describes salvation as a completed rescue whose full effects are awaited.

Salvation's origin is God's mercy, not human desire or effort. Augustinian and Reformed readers hold that this excludes any human contribution to God's choice, including the will to believe; Arminian and Wesleyan readers hold that it excludes human merit but not the response of faith that grace enables. Both agree that no one can claim mercy as a right.

Sonship, described in 8:14-17 as the privilege of all who are led by the Spirit, is here offered to those who were once outside God's people. The promise to Israel becomes the door through which Gentiles enter.
The last witness is the least likely one, and Paul presents his own calling as the clearest case of undeserved favor. The way he names himself anticipates verse 10.

Paul claims to have worked harder than all the others and in the same breath gives the credit to grace. Augustine appealed to this verse repeatedly in his writings against Pelagius: grace does not replace human effort but produces it, and the effort remains grace's fruit.

A Gentile was received as a brother without the sign of the covenant with Abraham. The acceptance of Titus is the practical form of the gospel Paul preaches: Gentiles belong to God's people through Christ, not by becoming Jews.
Grace and law as a way of righteousness are alternatives. To add the law as a condition of acceptance is not to supplement grace but to set it aside.
Redemption is liberation by payment: Christ bought his people out of the curse. Paul's language of buying back (4:5) sets salvation in the vocabulary of freedom from slavery.

Inheritance by promise and inheritance by law are mutually exclusive. What God gives as a gift cannot at the same time be earned by keeping commands, and Paul insists the inheritance was a gift from the start.
Forgiveness is the measure of grace's wealth, not of human worth. Paul describes grace as overflowing, lavished, not rationed to the deserving.
The perfect tense presents salvation as a secure present possession already given, not only a hope. Verse 8 will restate the same words with ‘through faith’ added.

This verse became a banner text of the Reformation. The Council of Trent (1547, session 6, chapter 8) also affirmed that nothing preceding justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of it, and the Lutheran-Catholic Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999) could affirm together that salvation is by grace alone. The traditions still differ on how faith, works, and the sacraments relate after that first grace.

Salvation here has a present and ongoing dimension. The verse does not make salvation a human achievement (verse 13 rules that out) but calls for its full outworking in a life of obedience and humility.
Salvation is pictured as a new exodus: rescue from one power and transfer under another. It is not self-improvement within the old domain but a change of lord.
Salvation is an inheritance, received as heirs of the Son who is ‘heir of all things’ (verse 2). The future orientation prepares the letter's call to hold on until the inheritance is received.
Salvation is called ‘so great’ because of who announced it. The verse also shows how the gospel was handed on: from the Lord, through eyewitnesses, to the next generation.
Salvation is described as being brought to glory, the destiny Psalm 8 described. Jesus is the pioneer who leads a family into it, not a solitary hero.
Those who failed had experienced the exodus. Rescue from Egypt did not guarantee arrival in the land, which is the point the author presses on readers who have experienced Christian beginnings.
Those who believe enter God's rest. The rest is received, not constructed; it is God's own completed rest, which he opens to his people.
Salvation is accompanied by things that can be seen: the work and love of verse 10. The author's confidence about his readers rests on those marks and, finally, on God's own faithfulness (verse 10).
Christ saves ‘completely’, and his saving work is not only past. His present intercession is part of salvation, as Romans 8:34 and 1 John 2:1 also teach.

The outcomes of shrinking back and of faith are destruction and the preservation of life. The author includes himself with the readers among those who believe, a pastoral verdict that answers the warnings of verses 26-31.

The books of deeds and the Book of Life stand side by side. Deeds are real evidence, and no one is judged on anything else; yet 21:27 calls the Book of Life the Lamb's, and 13:8 says the names were written there before the beast demanded worship. The verse holds together judgment by works and rescue by grace, as Paul does in Romans 2:6 and 3:23-24.
